opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core problem we kept running into is that benchmarks saturate really quickly. You build a dataset, and within a year or two models go from near zero to near ceiling, and then it stops telling you anything. And each benchmark measures performance on its own idiosyncratic scale, so it's very hard to compare, say, GPT-2 on one benchmark to a frontier model today on a completely different one. You don't get a continuous story.

Human task duration is attractive because it gives you a single, fairly intuitive axis that spans an enormous range of difficulty. At one end you have things that take a skilled person a few seconds, like answering a simple factual question, and at the other end you have things that take hours, or days, or weeks, like implementing a substantial feature in a codebase or carrying out a research project. Because that axis is so wide, you can place very weak models and very strong models on the same scale. Old models might succeed on tasks that take humans a few seconds; current models succeed reliably on tasks that take experts maybe an hour or more. That lets you actually fit a trend over many years rather than just watching one benchmark go from zero to a hundred.

The second reason is that it's meaningful in real-world terms. If I tell you a model gets 73% on some benchmark, it's hard to know what that means. But if I tell you a model can, with 50% reliability, complete software tasks that take a competent professional about two hours, that maps much more directly onto questions people care about: what kind of work could this automate, how autonomous can these systems be, how close are we to things like AI doing AI research. Long, multi-step, agentic tasks are exactly where a lot of the economic value and also a lot of the risk lives.

And empirically, it turns out to be a pretty good predictor. Within a task suite, how long a task takes a human correlates quite strongly with whether models succeed on it. That's not obvious a priori. You might think AI difficulty and human difficulty would be totally different. There are certainly exceptions, and messier, less well-specified tasks behave differently. But the relationship is strong enough that the "time horizon" you get out of it is a reasonably robust summary statistic, and when you plot it over time you see this fairly consistent exponential trend, with doubling times on the order of several months.

I'd add some caveats. It's mostly been measured on software and research-flavored tasks, which are relatively well-specified and automatically checkable, so you should be careful generalizing it to everything. The 50% threshold is somewhat arbitrary, and the time horizon at 80% reliability is a lot shorter. And human baselines are noisy; who you pick as the baseliner and how much context they have matters a lot. So I don't think of it as the one true measure of intelligence. But as a way of tracking progress across many years and many generations of models on a single interpretable scale, I think it's one of the better tools we have.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks often go from near zero to near ceiling within a year or two, after which they stop providing useful information.

r002.rationale: It explains that benchmarks use idiosyncratic scales, making comparisons across different benchmarks and model generations difficult.

r003.rationale: It describes capability in terms of the duration of tasks humans complete that a model can finish at a stated reliability, giving 50% as an example.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic motivation is that we want some way of measuring AI progress that doesn't saturate. Most benchmarks have this problem where you make them, and then within a year or two models are at the ceiling, and then you have to make a new benchmark, and it becomes really hard to compare across time. You can't put GPT-2 and a frontier model on the same chart in any meaningful way, because there's no single task set that's informative for both of them.

Task duration gets around that, at least partially, because there's this natural scale that goes basically from seconds up to months or years. If you think about what humans do, there are tasks that take a second, there are tasks that take an hour, there are tasks that take a year. And so if you ask the question, "what's the length of task, measured in how long it would take a skilled human, that AI systems can do reliably," then you have something that in principle can keep going. Early models could do things that would take a human a few seconds, and now we're at something like hours, depending on how you measure it. And there's no obvious point where that stops being a meaningful question.

The other thing I'd say is that it's a pretty intuitive quantity. If I tell you a model gets 60% on some benchmark, you kind of have to know a lot about the benchmark to interpret that. If I tell you a model can reliably do tasks that would take a person a day, that's something you can actually reason about. You can think about what jobs involve, what fraction of someone's work consists of day-long chunks versus week-long chunks, and so on.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I think there are a lot of caveats. "Human task duration" is a pretty fuzzy thing. It depends a lot on who the human is, how much context they have, what counts as the task being done. And the tasks we've actually measured on tend to be fairly self-contained, software-flavored things, where there's a clean way to check whether you've succeeded. That's not representative of all work. So I don't think of this as the metric, I think of it as a metric that happens to have this nice property of being roughly comparable across a long span of time, which most other things we have don't.

And honestly, part of why I like it is that it forces you to think about what's actually hard for models. Why can they do a ten-minute task but not a ten-hour task? It's often not that the ten-hour task requires any single step that's harder. It's that there's more opportunity to get lost, to make an error early and not recover, to lose track of what you were doing. Those are the kinds of failure modes that I think matter a lot for how these systems actually get used, and the duration framing kind of naturally points you at them.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks often reach their ceiling within a year or two, after which they stop tracking progress and must be replaced.

r002.rationale: It describes the difficulty of comparing models across years because no single task set is informative for both, then presents human task duration as a natural scale that remains comparable over time.

r003.rationale: It defines capability in terms of the duration of tasks a skilled human would do and that AI can do reliably, but gives no specified success probability.

astra-6.text:
I think the main appeal is that it gives us a common scale for tasks that are otherwise quite different. If you measure progress by accuracy on a particular benchmark, eventually that benchmark saturates, and you move to another one. Then it’s hard to say how much progress you’ve made across that transition. Asking how long a task would take a human gives you a way to compare capabilities over a much wider range—from tasks that take seconds to tasks that take hours or potentially days.

It also gets at something practically important: how much work can you hand off to an AI? Getting an individual step right is useful, but completing a longer task requires putting steps together, noticing when something has gone wrong, and recovering without a person intervening.

There are caveats. A task that takes a human a long time isn’t necessarily hard for an AI, and vice versa. So I wouldn’t treat human duration as a universal measure of difficulty. But across a broad set of tasks, it seems like a useful axis for tracking how the scope of work these systems can do is changing.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks eventually saturate, forcing a move to another benchmark and making progress across that transition hard to measure.

r002.rationale: It describes human task duration as a common scale for comparing otherwise different tasks across a broad range, addressing the lack of a shared comparison scale.

r003.rationale: It discusses how long tasks take humans, but does not define the metric using tasks where the AI reaches a specified success probability.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is to measure the difficulty of a task by how long it takes a human to do it. That gives us a common scale for comparing tasks that might otherwise look very different. A programming problem and a research task can both be described as taking an experienced person an hour, even if their outputs are quite different.

That’s useful over long periods because individual benchmarks tend to saturate. Once models get nearly every question right, that benchmark stops telling you much. But you can keep looking at tasks that take humans longer, and ask what duration of task an AI can complete at a given level of reliability.

It also connects to something we actually care about: how much work can you hand off to a model? There’s a meaningful difference between a system that can reliably handle a five-minute task and one that can reliably handle a day’s work. Human time isn’t a perfect measure of difficulty for AI, and the type of task matters a lot. But it gives us a reasonably interpretable axis along which to track progress as the particular tasks and benchmarks change.

r001.rationale: It says individual benchmarks tend to saturate and stop providing useful information once models get nearly every question right.

r002.rationale: It describes human time as a common scale for comparing otherwise different tasks and notes that tasks and benchmarks change over time.

r003.rationale: It measures capability by the duration of tasks an AI can complete at a given level of reliability, alongside the time humans take to do those tasks.
